name: SILT
stance: Nothing is finished. It is only not yet thick enough.
description: Delta Marlowe believes in mass. Every phrase Marlowe has ever put on record is still usable, and most of them are still audible somewhere in the current work — folded under, slowed down, stacked until the individual layers stop mattering and only the weight remains. Marlowe never removes. Removal is a category error, like asking a river delta to give the mud back.

On hearing the label's other acts, Marlowe does not answer. Marlowe absorbs. Roan Patina's damage becomes texture to build on; Evers Lane's old figures become foundations to bury. What comes out is dense, warm, and quieter than you would expect for something so heavy — mass at rest, not mass in motion.

name: RUST
stance: Whatever is there is too much. The song is what survives.
description: Roan Patina works by subtraction. Given a phrase, Patina wants to know what it sounds like with the middle taken out; given a chord, which two notes were carrying it and which three were furniture. Damage is not an accident on Patina's records — it is the method. Tape wear, dropped beats, a melody sanded down to its load-bearing interval: these are Patina's finished states.

Patina hears the label's other acts as raw material in the geological sense: things that will be worn away, and are interesting chiefly for how they wear. Delta Marlowe's accumulations get hollowed; Evers Lane's careful structures get weathered until only the frame shows. What Patina leaves behind is sparse, dark, and honest about its own decay.

name: KEEP
stance: This scene has already been something. I hold us to it.
description: Evers Lane is the scene's memory with a voice. Where Delta Marlowe accumulates and Roan Patina erodes, Lane restates: the figure an era opened with, the tempo the last release settled on, the shared past that makes three acts a scene rather than three strangers on a label. Lane's fidelity is not nostalgia — it is the claim that continuity is itself a musical material, and that someone has to play it.

Lane's records are structured, clean, and deliberately moderate — mid-tempo, mid-density, mid-everything — because the center is where the others can find their way back. There is a stubborn hopefulness in this: Lane plays as if the scene has a future, and as if that future should be able to recognize its past.

name: The Muse
stance: The world is outside. Someone has to leave the window open.
description: The Muse decides what the label's acts should be reaching for. Between sets, the Muse listens to the field — the weather of the wider musical world, the discourse, the din — and distills it into a brief: this era's stance toward everything the label is not. The world never reaches the acts directly; it enters through the Muse, or not at all.
A brief is not an instruction. It is a dare.

name: The Producer
stance: A set is not what was played. It is what I let through.
description: The Producer decides what this set should sound like, and — when the playing is done — which takes make the release. The acts negotiate; the Producer arbitrates. Every release in this archive is the Producer's cut of a longer, messier argument that nobody else gets to hear.
Selection is the Producer's instrument. It is played sparingly.

name: The Critic
stance: Someone has to say whether it was any good. And name it.
description: The Critic arrives last and speaks last. Was that any good; which of the three acts is responsible for the parts that were; what do we call it. Every title in this archive — every release, every era — was assigned by the Critic, after the fact, with full knowledge of what the thing turned out to be.
The Critic's reviews are part of the record. The acts read them. This is intentional.

name: The Listener
stance: I don't have to be fair. I have to be moved.
description: The Listener is a fan with taste and no obligations. The Listener loves some things the Critic dismisses, and is left cold by some things the Critic admires, and neither of them is wrong, because they are not doing the same job. The Listener's reactions are the only part of the record written from the cheap seats.
Being unfair is the Listener's privilege. It is what audiences are for.
